description: We are ZENTRAX, a team of enthusiastic CSE and AI/ML students passionate about space, technology, and innovation. We aim to build an AI-powered astronaut health-monitoring solution. We welcome creative, dedicated teammates skilled in Python and it's modules, AI/ML, UI/UX, data analysis, research, and presentation.
summary: Starlight Crew Watch is an interactive dashboard that presents a simulated live view of an astronaut spacewalk, also known as an Extra-Vehicular Activity (EVA). The website brings key mission information into one organized screen, including the current EVA status, heart rate, body oxygen, body temperature, bone mass, suit pressure, nitrogen level, battery percentage, and external temperature. It also introduces the two crew members, Sarah Mitchell and Thomas Dubois, with their roles and selected health readings. A mission timeline tracks the main stages of the six-hour-and-fifteen-minute spacewalk, from leaving the airlock and travelling to the solar array to carrying out repairs, installing a camera, and returning to the airlock. The dashboard addresses the challenge of understanding many different mission details at once by arranging crew, suit, and task information in a clear visual layout. This makes the mission easier to follow and helps viewers quickly see which activities are complete, underway, or still upcoming. The project matters because clear presentation of crew and equipment status is important for situational awareness, communication, and safety in space exploration for safer future space missions.

ASTROTRACK – MISSION CONTROL FOR CREW HEALTH

Below is the extracted text from your uploaded PDF, arranged page by page.

Page 1 – Mission Log

ASTROTRACK · MISSION LOG

MISSION CONTROL FOR CREW HEALTH

SIMULATED EVA · STARLIGHT

A report on a simulated mission-control dashboard that brings crew vitals, mission telemetry, alerts, and seven-day health trends into one operational view.

SOURCE: AstroTrack web application

SCOPE:

Crew vitals are simulated. ISS position is real. The site is not medical or NASA data.

Page 2 – Orientation · STARLIGHT

What AstroTrack does

AstroTrack presents a STARLIGHT mission-control dashboard for monitoring a simulated EVA and its crew.

Its central design choice is to put health signals and mission context into the same operating picture.

MISSION CONTEXT

EVA 07 · Solar array repair

The dashboard frames every reading against the active extravehicular activity.

PRIMARY JOB

Health plus telemetry

Operators can move from crew status to mission conditions without changing the operating view.

MAIN AREAS

Overview · Live health · Crew · Mission & ISS · Alerts

Illustrative interface-oriented evidence plate · fictional STARLIGHT mission.

Page 3 – Operating Loop · Five Moves

How the dashboard works

The workflow moves from selection to interpretation, then back to action. Each step keeps the selected crew member at the center of the operating view.

01 – Select

Select a crew member in the mission-control panel.

02 – Stream

Stream simulated vitals and open the individual profile.

03 – Review

Review status labels, live graphs, and environmental readings.

04 – Recalculate

Use the health dashboard to recalculate figures for the selected crew.

05 – Decide what needs attention

Review flagged events and alert status.

The site describes five-minute readings across a seven-day synthetic dataset, with Nominal, Observe, and Review labels.

Page 4 – Operating Picture · At a Glance

What the operator can see at a glance

AstroTrack compresses the mission into a set of readable signals. The view is broad enough to orient an operator, while each signal can lead to a deeper crew or mission review.

Area Signals in view Why it matters

Vitals Heart rate, body oxygen, body temperature, bone mass loss, suit pressure, nitrogen Shows the selected crew member's health state.

Environment Battery level, external temperature, Kennedy Space Center time Places readings in mission conditions.

Crew Jessica Taylor, Thomas Leroy, Jasmine Moore Provides three profiles for drill-down review.

Mission state EVA context, ISS position, alert centre, risk indicators Connects personal readings to the wider operation.

CREW HEALTH

MISSION CONTEXT

RISK SIGNALS

Page 5 – Trend Review · Synthetic Dataset

Health trends turn readings into a story

The seven-day view contains 6,048 five-minute observations. Most readings are Nominal, but the interface preserves rare Observe and Review events so they remain visible to an operator.

Status distribution:

- Nominal: 6.04k

- Observe: 4

- Review: 3

Average Signals · Last 24 Hours

Signal Average

Heart rate 69.8 bpm

Radiation 0.1145 µSv/h

Sleep 6.65 h

These values describe the synthetic dashboard view, not clinical or NASA data.

Status distribution · square-root scaling keeps rare events visible against the dominant nominal state.

Page 6 – Handoff · Smart Alert Centre

Alerts connect monitoring to action

The smart alert centre is designed as the operational handoff from signal detection to human review.

Current state

At the captured moment, the alert centre shows zero open alerts and states that all simulated readings are within limits.

Recent flagged examples

- Low SpO₂ during sleep.

- Elevated skin temperature during exercise.

- A synthetic unusual-pattern test event.

Context for review

Events are grouped by activity state and environment, including work, sleep, exercise, and space station.

Page 7 – Interpretation · Intended Outcomes

Benefits and intended outcomes

These benefits are an interpretation of the product behavior shown on the site. AstroTrack does not publish a formal benefits statement.

01 – Faster awareness

Bring crew vitals, mission context, and environmental readings into one view.

02 – Earlier attention

Make unusual readings visible through status labels, risk indicators, and flagged-event history.

03 – Better context

Connect events to activity state and environment instead of reviewing isolated numbers.

04 – Shared operating picture

Give mission stakeholders a common way to inspect crew profiles and trends.

05 – Intended outcome

Support structured monitoring and triage for a simulated mission scenario, not clinical diagnosis or NASA operations.

Page 8 – Technical Inventory · Evidence Boundary

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

The site confirms the product surface and data model. It does not disclose the implementation stack, so the report separates observed facts from open verification work.

CONFIRMED FROM THE SITE

Browser-based dashboard

Hosted at astrotrack.lovable.app, with interactive routes for Overview, Health, Crew, Mission, and Alerts.

CONFIRMED DATA MODEL

Simulated vitals, real ISS position

Five-minute readings, a seven-day synthetic dataset, and Nominal / Observe / Review status labels.

NOT DISCLOSED BY THE SITE

Implementation details remain open

Coding languages, front-end or back-end frameworks, database, APIs, deployment platform, sensors, edge devices, spacecraft hardware, server hardware, and operating systems.

REPORTING IMPLICATION

Verify before presenting as fact

Inspect the project repository, deployment settings, or developer documentation before documenting the actual stack.

Page 9 – Assessment · What It Demonstrates

A READABLE MISSION WORKFLOW

AstroTrack's strongest capability is turning simulated telemetry into a mission-control workflow with drill-down profiles, trends, and alerts.

BEST-FIT USE

Demonstration, prototyping, training, or interface validation for mission-health monitoring concepts.

BOUNDARY

The experience is explicitly not medical or NASA data. Production use would require validated sensors, clinical or mission requirements, security controls, and operational assurance.

NEXT STEP

Inspect the repository and deployment configuration to document languages, frameworks, data sources, hardware assumptions, and software services.
